As San Diego battles severe capacity bottlenecks and overnight line fatigue, Downtown Los Angeles offers the physical infrastructure and local talent to redefine modern fan gatherings. Here is why this year’s Halloween programming slate signals a major turning point for West Coast entertainment conventions.

Every year, San Diego Comic-Con dominates the conversation. It grabs every headline, floods our social feeds, and draws every major studio looking to drop big trailers. But every single year, the exact same question crosses my mind: why doesn’t the city that actually houses the heart of the entertainment world host an event that matches or beats it? That city is Los Angeles.

L.A. Comic Con is right around the corner, and it has quietly spent the last fifteen years building up something real. I still remember walking the floor during its first year under the original Comikaze banner when I covered conventions for a small outlet called Shifted2U. It was scrappy, energetic, and full of raw potential. Fifteen years later, it hasn’t quite reached the sheer scale of SDCC, but there isn’t any logical reason why it shouldn’t.

Downtown L.A. actually has every logistical advantage needed to fix what feels broken in convention culture right now.

Why doesn’t the entertainment capital of the world host an event that matches San Diego? Downtown Los Angeles has every structural advantage needed to fix what feels broken in convention culture.

Fixing the Bottlenecks: The Infrastructure Advantage

If you've ever attended San Diego Comic-Con, you know the grind. You're dealing with massive crowds, stress-inducing badge lotteries, and a parking situation that is an absolute nightmare. Then come the dreaded overnight campouts on the marina outside of Hall H. You suffer on the concrete just to see a single studio presentation for an “exclusive” three-minute trailer that inevitably leaks online within minutes of release. It turns catching a panel into an exhausting endurance test instead of something fun.

L.A. Comic Con doesn’t have to deal with any of that. The venue alone can solve those capacity headaches. The Los Angeles Convention Center features over 100,000 square feet of usable exhibit floor space across the massive West and South Halls. Between the upstairs and downstairs layouts, open staging areas, and dozens of extra rooms, the building has the room to handle heavy crowds without everything locking up.

Between multi-level show floors, dedicated staging halls, and breakout spaces, the Los Angeles Convention Center is built to absorb massive attendance without grinding to a halt.

Then look right outside the doors. You aren’t boxed into a narrow strip of land like the Gaslamp District. No, you’re sitting right in the center of Downtown Los Angeles. Right across the street is L.A. LIVE, with the Peacock Theater, the Crypto Arena, and major hotels like the J.W. Marriott. There’s plenty of space, stages, and spots to house an event that rivals anything on the West Coast without forcing fans to sleep on the pavement.

Main Stage Heavyweights: Bridging Cinema and Gaming

A huge venue doesn’t mean much without guests people actually want to see, and this year’s lineup shows L.A. Comic Con is making real moves. The guest list isn’t just about standard autographs. It connects what is happening in movies and TV directly to the gaming world.

Leading the pack on Saturday and Sunday is Nicolas Cage in his first-ever L.A. Comic Con appearance. Cage is an absolute legend whose career connects cult classics like Ghost Rider and National Treasure with projects like Spider-Noir. When you see characters like Ghost Rider showing up in games like Marvel Rivals, having Cage on stage feels perfectly timed.

The programming slate connects what is happening on theatrical screens directly to gaming culture, proving the convention is catering to how fans actually consume modern media.

The Star Wars side is just as big on Friday and Saturday with Hayden Christensen and Rosario Dawson. Seeing them together after their appearances in Ahsoka is huge, especially with season two on the horizon. Just like Cage, Christensen shows that crossover appeal, since Anakin Skywalker is just as big in games like Fortnite as he is on screen. The best part? You can actually sit in a panel room and hear them speak without having to camp outside for twenty hours.

On top of that, Bob Odenkirk is making his first convention appearance alongside Aaron Paul, Dean Norris, and Giancarlo Esposito. I hope Bryan Cranston surprises us as well, that would elevate what is already an incredible Breaking Bad reunion. Toss in the cast of Futurama after their recent run on Hulu, and you’ve got a stage lineup worth getting excited about.

Halloween Atmosphere and Floor Logistics

If you’re planning your trip, the details are simple. L.A. Comic Con runs from Friday, October 30 through Sunday, November 1, 2026, right at the Los Angeles Convention Center.

What makes this weekend extra special is that it lands directly on Halloween. The energy on the floor is going to be wild. Cosplayers spend months building out their gear for Halloween anyway, so having a full convention on that exact weekend means we’re going to see some incredible costume work.

Having a full convention land directly across Halloween weekend means the costume craftsmanship and creator energy on the show floor will be unmatched.

Beyond the main stage panels, the floor has plenty of areas to explore. Artist Alley is always a highlight, alongside dedicated gaming spaces, studio booths, and anime areas. Whether you’re picking up prints, checking out demos, or just checking out the cosplays, the layout gives everything room to breathe.

Why We Need to Elevate the Conversation

I’m genuinely excited to be on the ground for this. Walking the floor fifteen years ago when it was still starting out as Comikaze showed me what this event could become, and seeing how much it has grown since then is awesome.

The only way a show like this breaks out and gets the recognition it deserves is if we actually talk about it, share it, and show up. San Diego doesn’t need to have all the fun. Los Angeles has the talent, the studios right in its backyard, and the physical space to be a massive hub for pop culture.

San Diego doesn’t need to hold the monopoly on West Coast excitement. Los Angeles has the creative talent, the studio backing, and the physical room to lead the conversation.

title: Lanterns | The Grounded Blueprint for James Gunn’s DCU
excerpt: Halfway through its first season, this detective-driven series proves that restrained power scaling and character-focused storytelling are exactly what the new cinematic universe needs.
preview: I can’t believe we’re already at the halfway point of Lanterns. The season kicked off with a bang and has somehow gotten better every week. This series has done an incredible job of introducing us to the Green Lantern mythos. And, it fits perfectly into James Gunn’s new DCU while maintaining its own distinct identity.

One of the things I love most about Gunn’s approach is that every show and movie gets to stand on its own, yet still connect to the broader universe. I watch this and immediately know it belongs in the DCU. As someone who was never a Green Lantern fan, it’s crazy how much this show has completely drawn me in. Every week, I’m hyped with HBO Max launched and ready. The second the episode drops, I hit play.

That’s a great feeling, and it’s exactly what I want from the broader DCU. I want to feel this level of anticipation, not just for myself, but for the entire fanbase. I hope this prestige quality transcends Lanterns and sets the standard moving forward. Honestly, I’d love it if the team behind this series tackled Batman next.

I can’t believe we’re already at the halfway point of Lanterns. The season kicked off with a bang and has somehow gotten better every week. This series has done an incredible job of introducing us to the Green Lantern mythos. And, it fits perfectly into James Gunn’s new DCU while maintaining its own distinct identity.

One of the things I love most about Gunn’s approach is that every show and movie gets to stand on its own, yet still connect to the broader universe. I watch this and immediately know it belongs in the DCU. As someone who was never a Green Lantern fan, it’s crazy how much this show has completely drawn me in. Every week, I’m hyped with HBO Max launched and ready. The second the episode drops, I hit play.

The Hal and John Dynamic

That’s a great feeling, and it’s exactly what I want from the broader DCU. I want to feel this level of anticipation, not just for myself, but for the entire fanbase. I hope this prestige quality transcends Lanterns and sets the standard moving forward. Honestly, I’d love it if the team behind this series tackled Batman next.

As for this specific episode, the absolute highlight was watching Hal and John interact and build their relationship. Even if their partnership isn’t completely altruistic, they clearly each have their own motives, and it was really cool to see it flourish. We also saw the Guardians come down and deliver an ultimatum, telling John it is time to finally take the ring. John’s immediate reaction was basically “hold my beer.” I honestly thought he might say the phrase right there and force Hal to quickly pull the ring off his finger.

“In brightest day, in blackest night, no evil shall escape my sight. Let those who worship evil’s might, beware my power... Green Lantern’s light!”

You get a glimmer of hope for the future. If Hal survives, we’ll actually see them become real friends. I still hope they stay arrogant. I’ve been calling them lovable assholes in all my reviews, and I stand by that. I want them to keep that animosity and sharp banter, just from a place where they aren’t actively trying to kill each other.

The Sinestro Controversy

We have to address the elephant in the room. I took a lot of heat in the comments for being overly nitpicky about Sinestro’s initial design, but the actual execution of the character overrides any visual complaints. My favorite moments are not the heavy superhero elements or alien weaponry. Instead, the pure dialogue between Sinestro and Hal carries the entire narrative.

“The writing proves there is deep, unresolved tension in that relationship. Because of how rich those interactions are, I am completely convinced that Hal Jordan is not dead.“

I fully expect Sinestro to break out of prison, secure a yellow ring, and force a massive clash between himself, Hal, and John.

Pacing, Power, and Detective Work

Overall, it’s just crazy how good this show is. This is the exact level of premium storytelling we expect from HBO Max. Lanterns has four episodes left, airing every Sunday at 6:00 PM PST, and if you haven’t started it yet, you need to catch up. The pacing is tight, the character introductions are flawless, and it operates at a cinematic quality that rivals most theatrical releases right now.

The broader DCU needs to take notes from this creative team. My favorite moments are actually the quiet, dialogue-driven scenes. They aren’t relying heavily on CGI or overusing the rings. In fact, keeping the ring usage reserved makes it feel much more impactful. Instead, John and Hal are playing grounded detectives. Coming into this completely blind to the comic lore, I never realized the Lanterns operated as space cops solving mysteries.

The Zoe Reveal and HBO’s Mature Edge

The character reveals are hitting exactly as hard as the action. I figured out Zoe was a Manhunter from the very first episode just based on her slightly off demeanor. I originally expected Manhunters to be entirely emotionless, but watching her pretend to have human emotions to play the long game adds a fascinating layer to the mystery.

“Make no mistake, this is definitively not a kids’ show. Between John drawing a naked man and John’s “relationship” with Zoe, this series is proudly definitely an HBO Max show.”

We still have to wait to see Guy Gardner and figure out exactly how the 2016 timeline resolves, but the world-building is undeniably brilliant.

The Merch Hunt

The fan response has been incredible to watch. It’s connecting with people, sparking strong emotions, and doing exactly what these projects are designed to do: introduce a brand new audience to DC. That is how this franchise will eventually rise to compete with the MCU.

As much as I love Batman, I’ve never found myself hunting down props or toys. I grew out of collecting a long time ago. But this show literally has me scouring the internet for a Lantern ring. Check my search history and you’ll see countless Etsy shops and the official DC store. I’m genuinely about to drive up to Burbank to check the Warner Bros. Studio store just to see if they have my size in stock. Missing San Diego Comic-Con this year really stings because I could’ve easily snagged one there.

I am loving this show, and the quality is absolutely exceeding all expectations. If you want to dive deeper into the exact scenes that make this detective formula work, watch my full breakdown in the video below. What are your thoughts on the season so far? Let me know in the comments.

preview: When a studio decides to adapt a franchise this massive, the final product better be damn good, because we definitely don't need any more bad video game adaptations.

Sony Pictures and Reddit completely hooked it up. We grabbed some drinks and popcorn, and we got to sit in on a live Q&A with director Zach Cregger, hosted by Straw Hat Goofy. Seeing him run the panel in person was incredibly inspiring. I genuinely hope to get on his level one day.

Let's get right to the point. This movie is honestly great. Just 30 minutes of footage had me wanting more immediately. I was pissed when the screen cut to black. The LA Screening Experience

When a studio decides to adapt a franchise this massive, the final product better be damn good, because we definitely don't need any more bad video game adaptations.

Earlier this week, I drove all the way from Anaheim to LA to watch just the first 30 minutes of the new Resident Evil movie. It sounds ridiculous, but it was absolutely worth it. Sony Pictures and Reddit completely hooked it up. We grabbed some drinks and popcorn, and we got to sit in on a live Q&A with director Zach Cregger, hosted by Straw Hat Goofy. Seeing him run the panel in person was incredibly inspiring. I genuinely hope to get on his level one day.

Why Zach Cregger is the Perfect Fit

Let's get right to the point. This movie is honestly great. Just 30 minutes of footage had me wanting more immediately. I was pissed when the screen cut to black. I was hoping they'd surprise us and let the LA crowd watch the rest of the film, but we need to talk about the panel and how Zach Cregger's mind works.

Cregger directed Weapons, which legitimately sits right behind Obsession as one of my two favorite horror movies of all time. If there's one person who I feel could properly adapt Resident Evil, it's Zach Cregger, especially after watching Weapons.

This new Resident Evil balances elements of humor while still managing to be terrifying. It actually got me with a legitimate jump scare.

It's very rare for horror movies to actually work on me, so it felt incredible to physically react while watching it in a theater.

The Player's Perspective

So, how does it compare to the games and the older movies? A lot of people are already complaining that it isn't a direct 1:1 adaptation of the video games. Honestly, I don't care. I play the games, but I wouldn't call myself a die-hard fan. However, as a gamer, I can tell you this for a fact: this film feels more like a video game than any of the previous movies ever did.

Hear me out. When you watch the lead, played by Austin Abrams, navigate this world, you're watching him react exactly how a real player would.

Gamers love to act tough, but if we actually stepped into Raccoon City, we'd be the most ridiculous, bumbling idiots to exist.

Abrams isn't some elite marksman right out of the gate. He isn't great with guns, and his genuine reaction is basically, "What the f*** is going on here?" It feels incredibly immersive to experience this nightmare from the perspective of someone who's just as terrified and confused as we'd be.

The Marketing Strategy

I also have to compliment the marketing team. I'm a big proponent of avoiding trailers because they give away way to much of the plot, but the Resident Evil marketing has been brilliant! A majority of what has been shown in the trailers was pulled from the first 30 minutes of the movie. That gives me a lot of hope and anticipation for what we will see in the remaining hour of the movie. Admittedly, PlayStation did drop a new spot which was not in what I saw, but even that was just a single, scene that doesn’t give too much away.

Resident Evil Is Here

Resident Evil hits theaters on September 18, 2026. You should absolutely go see this in IMAX! People are going to be laughing, jumping, and having a blast. It's going to feel like playing a horror game in a crowded theater.

excerpt: By leveraging Netflix to broadcast their first true look at Vice City, Rockstar engineered a massive cultural moment that proved the streaming giant is ready to dominate interactive
preview: Netflix and Rockstar Games just made history. GTA VI, the follow-up to GTA V, which came out 13 years ago, is finally on the horizon, and we just got our real first look.

I said this when I first saw some the leaked footage: “the leaks do not matter.” First, Rockstar Games is still working on GTA VI, and they’ll likely be working on it until the last second. They want to ship something that’s going to be great, but they also wanted the people who see the game for the first time to see it at its highest possible quality. And that’s exactly what they did with the Netflix first look.
The lighting, the interaction with NPCs, the driving mechanics, the hair physics; everything about the city actually looked f***ing spectacular.

I’ve been against the leaks since they started. I’ve been saying it from the beginning: that whole “Robin Hood” narrative that Cyberleeks was pushing was absolute BS. It was a glorified crypto scam, and that’s the last bit of attention I’ll give it.

If you’ve been around for a while, you remember E3. It was a massive gaming event where the entire industry came together to showcase the future of gaming. Ever since E3 stopped, I’ve been wanting something that felt like E3 again. Even though this stream was dedicated to one game, it still brought back that feeling of attending or watching E3.

The lighting, the interaction with NPCs, the driving mechanics, the hair physics; everything about the city actually looked f***ing spectacular.

I’ve been against the leaks since they started. I’ve been saying it from the beginning: that whole “Robin Hood” narrative that Cyberleeks was pushing was absolute BS. It was a glorified crypto scam, and that’s the last bit of attention I’ll give it.

If anyone can revive E3, Netflix can.

If you’ve been around for a while, you remember E3. It was a massive gaming event where the entire industry came together to showcase the future of gaming. Ever since E3 stopped, I’ve been wanting something that felt like E3 again. Even though this stream was dedicated to one game, it still brought back that feeling of attending or watching E3.

Rockstar and Netflix delivered something that felt like E3 all over again.

If any studio has the ability to recreate that scale, it’s definitely Netflix. Think about it. Netflix doesn’t just dominate traditional streaming anymore. They’re aggressively expanding their footprint. They have a dedicated gaming division now, and they’re completely taking over live broadcasting. They’re streaming the SAG Awards live and pushing boundaries with massive interactive shows. It goes way beyond the digital screen, too. They have permanent physical event spaces and incredible on-the-ground activations.

I’ve personally attended their Emmy’s events, red carpet movie and streaming premieres, and exclusive pop-ups. Having experienced those activations, I can tell you firsthand that their production value is above all other studios. They have the infrastructure and the global reach to turn a single game trailer into a massive cultural moment. It really begs the question: what can’t they touch? I think this GTA VI showcase is the start of something much bigger than any of us realize.

What makes this even wilder is that Rockstar rarely had an appearance at E3. Rarely could a studio or publisher get them to showcase on stage. Yeah, sure, PlayStation got a few GTA V marketing plugs across the previous console generations but we never received a true first look of this scale.

So, how does GTA VI look?

GTA VI LOOKS F***ING INCREDRIBLE!

The gameplay mechanics, everything about it has me at a hype level that is actually surprising me because I’m not the biggest Grand Theft Auto fan. Yes, I play every game! But it feels like required gaming. I mean, who hasn’t played GTA?

Grand Theft Auto is not just a video game; it is massive virtual experience that sets the standard for the industry.

I remember playing GTA V with a girlfriend who hated videos games and she was surprisingly loving it. It had always a been really cool experience just to see how other people played and reacted to Grand Theft Auto. GTA V was a cultural juggernaut, but GTA VI is going to be a whole other level.

Don’t look at Grand Theft Auto as just a video game. Look at it as an experience. To me, GTA VI is the start of something that’s going to last for at least the next decade, maybe even longer. Rockstar Games didn’t put this much time and development into making something that’s only going to be around for a year.

I’m expecting this to be a massive expansive world the likes we’ve never seen before in gaming.

What have we learned about GTA VI?

Rockstar Games revealed details on the map size, and we now know the GTA VI map will be approximately three times as large as Red Dead Redemption 2 and two times as large as GTA V.

There are even relationship mechanics we’ll be able to work out, and there’s a lot of stuff in this game we don’t even know about yet! I’m sure we’re going to be exploring and finding out so much more.

Hyped enough to buy a PS5 Pro. If I even can.

I’m going to be playing and streaming it, and I’m hyped. I may even buy a PS5 Pro just to be able to play this at full quality. Can we talk about that for a second, though? GTA VI was shown with gameplay from the base-level PS5. They’ve been really specific about pointing out the fact that it was the PS5. If it looked this good on the base model PS5, how is it going to look on the PlayStation 5 Pro? Or the eventual next-gen consoles and PC?

What happened to the PlayStation Blackout?

That brings up an interesting reality check though. Shortly after this reveal, reports confirmed that the PS5 Pro sold out completely. Some people tried to dispute it, saying that’s just because of low stock, but selling out instantly proves there’s massive demand. This is happening right in the midst of the alleged “PlayStation blackout”, which really begs the question: was any of it even real, or was it just a hate and harassment campaign? The leaks didn’t matter, and performative online boycotts certainly didn’t stop the hardware from flying off the shelves.

Did RockStar Games Just Win GOTY?

Rockstar Games has cemented itself as a leader in the gaming industry. They set the standard for what games can and should be, and I think a lot of developers are going to be playing this and learning how to implement new things to create expansive worlds just like it.

I've had a worry. With The Game Awards returning on December 10th, shortly after the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, could it even win Game of the Year? I mean, is there even enough time? This reveal completely sold it for me, though. We might as well crown it Game of the Year right now just from the showcase alone. What could even top what we've just witnessed?

If you couldn’t tell, I’m looking forward to playing Grand Theft Auto 6 when it releases on November 19, 2026. I can’t believe it’s finally here. It was a long wait, but it was worth it. Rockstar Games isn’t just dropping a highly anticipated sequel; they are setting the foundation for the next decade (or longer) of interactive entertainment, and this Netflix showcase proved they are ready to own it.

The trailer Marvel just released literally gave me goosebumps. I was one of the fans who did the 22-movie Marvel Marathon in 2019, and I’ve still got my T-shirt right here to prove it. Living in the Regal Irvine Spectrum theater for three days was an unforgettable experience. It was an experience where I legitimately got hemorrhoids. Sorry if that’s TMI, but it’s the truth. Despite the physical toll on my body, I somehow still found a way to have a great time. And I gained a whole new community of friends all while living in a movie theater.

The Return of the Theatrical Event

I haven’t felt that same level of goosebumps since seeing the portal scene on opening night. Those chills just made waves throughout my entire body.

Regardless of what people say about Marvel, DC, comic book adaptations, and how much they whine about “comic book movie fatigue,” there’s absolutely no doubt about one thing. The Marvel Cinematic Universe gave those of us who grew up watching, reading, and playing these franchises something we never got before: genuine quality films.

You can argue that since Endgame, the studio hasn’t been hitting on all cylinders. I completely agree with you. I used to go into an MCU movie thinking, “This is going to be a hit, and this is something we’re going to be talking about for months on end.” Then we got films like Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania and Captain America: Brave New World.

But even with those missteps, you can’t deny that the buildup to Endgame was unprecedented. We had never seen a 22-movie franchise build up to a massive cultural event like that. I look back across the years and think about how my life has changed, how much I’ve grown as a person, and how I essentially grew up with this franchise.

Honestly, for some younger fans, this universe is all they know. Some people were born when Iron Man started, and they grew up right alongside the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Avengers: Endgame Encore is Marvel’s way of celebrating that legacy. They’re marketing it as a chance for all of us to relive those theater moments together. We get to laugh, cry, cheer, and just go for a ride with this epic all over again.

The Box Office Battle

Admittedly, I wasn’t too excited at first. It really begs the question: where is this so-called comic book movie fatigue?

While I already dropped a quick review of the first episode, I simply can’t stop thinking about this show. I have admittedly already watched episode one three times this week alone and we definitely need to dig deeper into why this show works so well.

A Radically Mature Tone

Let’s start with the tone. When parents see a new DC show, they likely assume it’s safe for their kids to watch. I mean, I knew going in that Lanterns was aiming for an older demographic, but the marketing didn’t fully reveal just how mature it would be. It looked like a serious take on the comic-book franchise, maybe PG-13 at a best. Instead, we got a gritty, adult-oriented detective story.

Spoilers are going to follow, so consider yourself warned.

The first episode kicks off with a sex scene. It isn’t too graphic, but it sets the baseline immediately. From there, the episode is packed with violence, action, and a lot of cursing. It isn’t quite a hard R rating, but parental supervision is definitely advised.

As someone who grew up watching DC movies and shows, I’m glad to see the universe actually maturing with its audience. We already have the animated shows for the younger audience, and those are great. But adults deserve our own corner of the franchise.

A Cast of Lovable Assholes

Tone aside, the character work in this episode is truly exceptional. Every single person on screen piqued my interest. Which is great because we need a solid cast to actually hold our intrigue as this mystery unfolds.

I’m fascinated by the central mystery. Who are the actual antagonists? Is it the aliens? Is it the rancher family that bailed Hal Jordan out of jail? I love that I genuinely don’t know what’s going to happen. I don’t follow the comics and I don’t even know if this is adapting a comic story line. So, I’m going into this completely blind with the rest of you.

Every character leaves you asking questions. Is the sheriff’s grandson foreshadowing something bigger? Will the sheriff herself have an expanded role in the DCU? While a second season hasn't officially been green-lit (no pun intended) yet, if these viewership numbers hold, we can definitely expect more Lanterns. I really hope it happens because I'd love to see these characters interwoven into the broader DCU.

What really stands out is that everyone in this series is deeply flawed. Frankly, they’re all kind of unlikable. There are no perfect, goody-two-shoes heroes here. They just feel like real, messy people, and that makes the show incredibly engaging, authentic and relatable.

The Setting, The Score, and The Law

The world-building is equally fantastic. If you haven’t looked into the original score by Stephanie Economou, you need to do so immediately. The music is incredible and really does a good job of matching this part of the world in the DCU. I’ve been listening to it nonstop and throwing it into the background of my short-form videos.

The setting itself feels real and grounded. I love how the court case played out. It established exactly why Hal and John can’t just fly (well, why Hal can’t) away to escape their problems. They actually have to follow the law. It sets up a world where superheroes exist everywhere, and even Space Cops aren’t above the law. The comedic timing in the courtroom, where Hal announces himself as the Green Lantern and the judge simply replies, “And?”, was perfect.

Also, those Green Lantern rings look freaking awesome! I definitely need to get my hands on a replica.

The 10-Year Time Jump

Now, we have to talk about that twist.

Massive spoilers to follow, but if you got this far, you should know that.

I was truly shocked to see that Hal Jordan is dead (or is he? He looked pretty dead to me). The marketing team deserves a massive round of applause. The trailers did a brilliant job of only showing us what we now realize are flashbacks. The entire first episode is set in 2016, and then the final moments jumps ten years into the future.

In 2026, John Stewart doesn't seem to have the ring, and it looks like Hal never actually passed it on. This opens up a massive mystery. Who killed Hal Jordan? Is he even really dead? Look, he's probably dead, but I'm allowed to have hope.

We are clearly getting two distinct storylines moving forward: the past and the present. This dual narrative is an awesome way to explore how John and Hal’s relationship progressed, and ultimately, how it devolved. Did they have a massive falling out? How did John become so cozy with the sheriff in the present day? There are so many unanswered questions.

The Golden Age of DC

I will absolutely be reviewing every single episode week to week as they drop on Sundays at 6:00 PM PST on HBO Max.

I genuinely love where the DCU is heading. We are getting a variety of adult-focused shows and broader blockbuster movies like Superman and Supergirl. Despite all the online discourse around James Gunn, I am a massive fan of the strategy.

With projects like Clayface, Man of Tomorrow, and the upcoming animated project Dynamic Duo on the horizon, the future is looking good for DC fans. We haven’t even seen the new Batman yet. And I’ll say it again, Comic Book fatigue is a myth; people just want good stories.

Does a movie with a viral marketing campaign like having people live in a billboard live up to the hype? Here is my review for The Last House.

The Last House is billed as a sci-fi thriller on Netflix, and the premise of this film is not what I expected in the slightest.

The Stiff Setup

This movie gets right into it from the start, introducing a blended family who will be trapped in this old, decaying home. Even though it kicks off immediately, I still had four false starts when trying to watch this film. The aspect of the movie that is arguably the most important was the weakest: the family dynamic.

“How are we expected to stay trapped in this house for 112 minutes if even the family doesn’t want to be there?”

The family dynamic itself just didn’t feel genuine. I was confused as to whether it was a stepfather situation or a marriage in decline. Either way, the acting among them felt stiff. We are talking about a cast that includes Greta Lee and Wagner Moura, actors I have seen deliver incredible performances before, but here there was just no chemistry. It took me by surprise to see them feel so wooden early on, and it had me genuinely concerned. The kids, while they do have a few amusing moments, were no better. I question who wrote the daughter to act like a 40-year-old woman from such an early age.

Does the acting get any better, or did I just stick it out? The acting does get a bit better as the story progresses, but that initial stiffness remains, only replaced by a somewhat more interesting premise. Usually, especially with Netflix, I will give up after the first try if a movie doesn’t hold my attention. But I gave this movie four chances! All because the viral marketing campaign had me thinking, “There has to be something more to this.” And I was right, because the premise shifts just in time to make me glad I somehow stuck it out.

The Thematic Shift

Without spoiling anything, there is a specific point where things really take a turn. It shifts from a film about a family coming together under terrible circumstances to a pure survival story featuring some clear mental decay. The premise set up by the marketing becomes something else entirely.

“It evolves into a message about how humans negatively impact nature and society, suggesting that if something else took over, maybe it would be for the better.”

I won’t dig into that too much because I don’t want to give it away. If you predicted what they are essentially fighting against, let me know in the comments, because it definitely caught me off guard.

The story tries to dabble in some mythos and fantasy elements that don’t really go anywhere. Instead, we finish off with the family essentially having a Home Alone-style battle. But honestly, it ends at a place that is much better than I expect from most Netflix originals. I didn’t know how they would close this film out, and just as the premise surprised me, the ending surprised me too.

The Verdict

My biggest issue with writing this review is trying to avoid spoilers. I want you to go on this ride the same way I did: zero expectations, total confusion, and just wondering, “How will this end?”

Overall, I thought it was a great movie that belongs on streaming. My expectations for Netflix movies tend to be low, but they did a good job on the film and an absolutely incredible job on the marketing campaign. Netflix may have just found its new hook! This is one of the few Netflix movies I can see myself rewatching, and that is saying a lot.

The gaming community is locked in a state of outrage. Since PlayStation announced its plan to move to an all-digital release model in January 2028, social media has been filled with angry posts and community notes.

At first this could have been a unified movement for consumer rights, but instead it devolved into a hate and harassment campaign.

Influencer Agenda and Aimless Toxicity

First, we saw influencers disingenuously latch onto the outrage to farm engagement. Small creators took the opportunity to ride the algorithm and grew their followings exponentially in a matter of days. The lack of authenticity became obvious when many of these accounts backpedaled, admitting they would still play the boycotted games and consoles because they needed to do it for their jobs.

This performative outrage fueled a growing wave of online toxicity. The movement is now entirely aimless. If you don’t align perfectly with their anger, you’re immediately attacked. Even early supporters of the boycott who admitted they still wanted to play upcoming massive releases were harassed by anonymous accounts.

Denying Facts and Data

The numbers don’t lie.

When the actual market data was released, it proved exactly why physical media is being phased out. We’re entering a phase which started with the film industry, where massive retailers like Best Buy and Target began pulling physical discs from store shelves.

The numbers don’t lie. Modern consumers prioritize convenience over everything else, and digital sales have skyrocketed. Recent U.S. data showed that only seven major games have sold over 100,000 physical copies this year.

Gamers in the community disingenuously attacked this metric making false claims against it and claiming that the post didn’t disclose data that was clearly disclosed. And those who acknowledge the data, but argued against it said “it only accounts for the U.S. sales market”, but that completely ignores the reality. The U.S. is among the two biggest gaming economies, only second to China.

If we factor in China, and their massive footprint in the global gaming economy, the physical data becomes astronomically worse. Physical console media in the Chinese market is practically nonexistent, as their multi-billion-dollar infrastructure is built entirely around digital, PC and mobile distribution.

Instead of accepting reality, parts of the community resorted to spreading misinformation, disinformation and generating fake AI data to counter the facts. We cannot argue with global consumer behavior and smart business decisions nor should anyone bother with disingenuous arguments.

GTA VI Leaks: Who does this hurt?

The most pressing example of this toxic entitlement is the recent Grand Theft Auto 6 leak. Seeing gameplay leak this close to the upcoming Netflix announcement is really disappointing, especially for the devs who put so much work into this.

Some people online claim these leaks are justified because the hacker claims it’s in the name of fighting for physical media, hint: it’s not. But I wonder, who does this strike against corporate greed and decisions actually impact?

As someone who has worked in the gaming industry for 13+ years most recently as a Junior Software Engineer and QA Tester at Sony Interactive Entertainment, I can tell you exactly who this hurts. It does not harm the corporate executives, and it definitely won’t change our inevitable digital-only future. It only hurts and disrespects the developers who have poured years of their lives into developing GTA VI. And, it only ruins the experience for people who have waited years to experience the game spoiler free.

With all this in mind, I question who, how and why would anyone support any of this? There is absolutely zero justification for it.

UPDATE: While writing this article the hacker has made new threats to leak additional content if their demands are not met.

The Real Battle: Digital Rights

Gamers need to mature and shift their focus. Throwing a fit on the internet because the market is changing does not help anyone. We can’t argue with the reality of consumer behavior. The silent majority has clearly already voted with their wallets and digital convenience won.

Not everything is black and white. I don’t want to see physical media disappear. I support having options to choose between physical and digital media. But, if we are rapidly moving into a digital future, we need to focus our energy on something that actually matters.

We should be fighting for concrete digital rights, a true system of digital ownership, and ensuring that the games we buy cannot simply be taken from us.

We can demand better systems without resorting to harassment, and the path for this is through actual legislation. A perfect example of this is happening now through the California with Assembly Bill 1921, also known as the “Protect Our Games Act.”

“When consumers organize legally and push for concrete rights, actual change happens”

The backlash against Ubisoft delisting The Crew, triggered a legislative campaign and it actually passed! This bill was passed by the State Assembly with bipartisan support. How often does that happen?

It imposes strict new rules on publishers, requiring them to provide a two month notice before shutting down a game. It also forces companies to offer solutions, either a playable offline version, a community server patch, or a full refund.

While the current drafted bill only applies to paid digital games released on or after January 1, 2028, it’s a massive step in the right direction. All of this proves that when consumers organize, the right way, legally and push for concrete rights, actual change can happen. Screaming and whining at community managers on social media accomplishes nothing, but passing a state law forces the entire industry to adapt.

A Better Solution: The Right to Archive

I was recently discussing the switch to digital media with a former coworker from PlayStation and I started workshopping a concept to resolve all of this. I believe that if publishers are going to stop providing access to physical media, then the community must be given the legal right and access to archive and print their own.

Building a system where users can back up their digital media to physical devices would be difficult and it definitely opens up a lot of piracy concerns. The complex conversations and new security processes to combat piracy would be a massive undertaking. But, providing a secure method for us to back up our games is only right since the companies want to remove our ability to buy and physical media in the first place.

We can demand true, real digital ownership without toxic hate and harassment campaigns. It’s time we start fighting the right battles.

What are your thoughts on the push for digital ownership? Would you support a legal archiving system if it meant giving up store bought physical discs?

I’ve seen this movie twice now, and that’s the first thing you should probably know, because it’s the thing that surprised me the most. I don’t do that often. I usually see a movie, form my take, and move on to the next one. I just got IMAX tickets today, because the IMAX screenings finally opened up. I’m considering Dolby 3D. And I’m still hunting for a ScreenX showing, which I’ll get into, because that’s actually a much bigger story than it sounds like.

Let’s Talk About the Box Office

Spider-Man: Brand New Day opened at $360 million domestically, and that is the biggest domestic opening weekend in history. It passed Avengers: Endgame, which had $357.1 million, and that’s a record I honestly figured was going to sit there forever.

Worldwide, it pulled $932 million in its opening weekend, which makes it the second biggest global opening of all time behind Endgame‘s $1.223 billion.

I do want to be clear about what these numbers actually are, because opening weekend records and all-time box office records are two very different things. Endgame is still sitting at around $2.79 billion lifetime. Brand New Day has a long way to climb before it’s anywhere near that conversation. But the opening itself is genuinely historic, and the part that impresses me the most isn’t the number. It’s how it happened.

It did all of that without IMAX.

Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey had exclusive rights to IMAX screens in North America for three weekends, which meant Sony was locked out of the biggest premium format in the business during the exact window when a Spider-Man movie needs it most. And The Odyssey wasn’t slowing down either. That film has cleared $911 million after three weekends, and it still took second place this weekend with $51 million. So this wasn’t a case of Spider-Man having the box office to itself. Two enormous movies were running at the same time, and one of them had the premium screens.

Sony broke the domestic opening record anyway.

The ScreenX Thing, Which I Think Is the Real Story Here

Here’s how they got around it, and I think this is the most interesting industry story of the summer.

Sony and CJ 4DPLEX created something called “Shot for ScreenX,” and Brand New Day is the first film in history that was actually shot for the format. That means a second unit was on set during production capturing the footage that plays on the side walls, instead of taking the finished movie and stretching the image out digitally in post. Destin Daniel Cretton has talked about the ScreenX team physically being there on set to shoot those wings.

That’s the IMAX playbook, applied to a format that has spent years being treated as a novelty upcharge on your ticket.

Think about what actually happened there. Nolan spends a decade turning IMAX into a real filmmaker’s format, shoots The Odyssey entirely on IMAX cameras, and locks up the screens. Sony can’t compete on that ground, so instead of just eating the loss, they went and built a rival premium format from the ground up and made their movie the first native release in it.

That’s not a marketing gimmick to me. That’s a studio getting squeezed and responding by creating a new category. And if “Shot for ScreenX” catches on with other filmmakers—and CJ 4DPLEX has said they’re already working with other studios on it—this is going to be the movie that started it.

IMAX has now confirmed that Brand New Day is coming to their screens as The Odyssey‘s exclusivity window closes, and the two films are going to share digital IMAX locations across America. I bought tickets the moment I saw the announcement. I know it’s not true IMAX 70mm, and I’m not going to pretend otherwise. But I still found myself thinking I have to go see this in IMAX, partly to support the movie, and partly because I just want to be in that room again.

The Video Game Thing

Okay, so this is the take that I think a lot of gamers can relate to.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day plays like a video game and feels like Marvel’s first video game adaptation.

It is not officially adapting Insomniac’s Spider-Man or Spider-Man 2. But I sat in that theater for two hours and twenty-five minutes, and I could not stop thinking about those games. Not for a single stretch of the movie. The entire time I was going, “I did that move in this game,” or “I know this reference, I’ve seen this before.”

The way Peter interacts with the police. The traversal. The rhythm of the fights. Even the little things, like the apparel, which is pulled almost directly out of the game in ways that are not subtle at all. If you’ve put twenty hours into those games, you’re going to feel it constantly.

And I mean all of that as a compliment.

Here’s why. Outside of the comics, I think the Insomniac Spider-Man games told the most emotional and the strongest stories in all of modern Spider-Man entertainment. Not only the best action, but yes, the best stories as well. And a big part of that is that those games had twenty-plus hours to build out an expansive world, let the characters breathe, and actually earn their emotional beats. That’s a structural advantage a two-hour movie should never be able to compete with.

Somehow, Brand New Day does the exact same thing in 145 minutes, and I still don’t fully understand how.

Tom Holland has said he was in the writers’ room on this one, and I believe him, because you can feel it in the movie. If you’ve been following his interviews the way I have, he brings up the PlayStation 5 Spider-Man 2 game constantly. He’s an actual gamer. He knows this character. And more than that, he listens to the people who love this character, which is not something you can say about everybody who’s played a comic book role.

So if this ever crosses his feed, I’ll just say this much: Adapt Spider-Man 2. And keep an eye on whatever Insomniac ends up doing with Spider-Man 3.

I also really hope Insomniac Games gets the credit here. You can argue the influence went both directions—that the movies inspired the games and the games inspired the movies—and honestly, the synergy between them is one of the coolest things about all of this. But the DNA of those games is on that screen, and Insomniac built something that genuinely changed how this character moves and feels. A record-breaking movie is now running on that foundation, and I think that deserves to be said out loud.

Is the Movie Overstuffed?

For me personally, the answer is no, and I went in fully expecting it to be.

I felt like I enjoyed every single cast member, and if anything, my complaint runs the other way, because I just wanted more of some of them. If I had to say who this movie is really about, it’s Spider-Man and Punisher. Everything else orbits around those two.

The Hulk material that you saw in the trailer is in there, but it’s a smaller presence than the marketing led me to expect. Ned and MJ are also in it a surprisingly small amount. But none of that is a bad thing. If anything, less is more here. I was happy every time they showed up on screen, and that’s exactly the reaction you want out of an ensemble movie and almost never actually get.

What I appreciated the most is that this movie actually deals with the fallout of No Way Home. Peter is living in a world that doesn’t remember him, and that’s the kind of premise a lot of movies would nod at in the first ten minutes and then quietly walk away from. This one doesn’t. There are real consequences, and it sits in them.

Going into it, I was wondering whether they were going to handle that or dodge it. They handled it, and they handled it well, and I think moving forward the relationships between Peter, MJ, and Ned are going to flourish again in a way that actually feels earned instead of reset.

The MCU Connection, and That Post-Credits Scene

Going into this movie, one of the things I was thinking about most was how connected it was going to be to Doomsday and Secret Wars. Were we going to get a Doctor Doom cameo? Some kind of big setup?

The answer is no, and I think that’s one of the best decisions the movie makes. It’s a really grounded, street-level film that’s confident enough to just be its own thing instead of spending its third act doing homework for the next movie.

The post-credits scene, though. I have to be absolutely honest with you: that is one of the most disappointing post-credits scenes in Marvel history. I felt like I wasted my time sitting there for it. Wait around at your own leisure, but I could have just watched a bad YouTube video about it and lost nothing.

That said, underneath the surface, this movie plants something significant. One of the most important elements of the MCU gets introduced here, and I genuinely think what happens in this film is going to have lasting effects that run through the entire phase after Secret Wars.

When I first saw it, I thought nobody was talking about this. I’ll own that I was wrong there, because three days into wide release everybody is talking about it. What I’ll say instead is that I don’t think people are weighing it correctly yet. There’s a difference between noticing that something happened and understanding what it’s going to cost down the line.

I’m doing a full breakdown and spoiler review of exactly what this means on the channel. Watch the video below, and if you enjoy the coverage, make sure you hit subscribe so you don’t miss the next one!

Seeing It With a Crowd

Both times I saw this movie, the audience was completely locked in.

Not phones out, half paying attention. Actually engaged. Reacting, laughing, applauding. That communal thing that streaming can’t replicate and that people keep announcing is dead.

There was also a pop-up event at the Regal Irvine Spectrum where they gave away posters and shir

ts, plus a photo op with Spider-Man. I got the poster, I missed out on the shirts. All of that footage should be live on my channel right now.

I bring it up because the marketing and the promotion around this release has been a masterclass. Sony didn’t just sell a movie, they built an event around going to see one. I really hope future Marvel movies, and honestly future movies in general, take note of how effective that was, because I think this is going to set the standard for how comic book movies get released going forward.

Rankings, and My Recency Bias

I have to be upfront about something here.

Every time I watch a Spider-Man movie, I realize I have recency bias. I like the most recent Tom Holland Spider-Man movie every single time I see it. The same thing happened with Andrew Garfield, and I told people that at the time. So take everything that follows with that in mind.

Spider-Man isn’t my favorite Marvel character. He never has been. He’s great, and I love seeing him on the big screen, and I get excited every time one of his movies comes out. So for me to now say Spider-Man: Brand New Day is my favorite MCU movie is a big deal.

In terms of Spider-Man specifically, though, my personal favorites are still Into the Spider-Verse and Across the Spider-Verse. Nothing has touched those two for me.

But Brand New Day is now my favorite live-action Spider-Man movie, and I’m including every Sony live-action entry and every MCU Spider-Man film before it. Tom Holland is officially my favorite Spider-Man.

And here’s the part I genuinely did not expect to be typing: I think this might be one of my favorite live-action comic book movies of all time. That means it’s beating out Batman, and I am a crazy Batman fan. It’s beating out Deadpool. If it weren’t for the Spider-Verse movies, I would absolutely be calling this my favorite Spider-Man movie ever made.

I’m going to rewatch the entire franchise and do a proper ranking, because I want to make sure I’m not just riding the high off two viewings in a week. But the fact that I want to go back a third time, and I’m still chasing a ScreenX showing, and I bought IMAX tickets the same day they were announced, tells me something that the numbers can’t.

Where This Leaves Us

We’re four movies into this version of Spider-Man, and it somehow feels like the start of something new.

That’s the strangest and best thing about Brand New Day to me. Sony and Marvel essentially rebooted the Spider-Man franchise without having to recast Spider-Man. The title isn’t just a comics reference; it’s an accurate description of what the movie actually does.

Marvel is having a crazy year. Tom Holland, Zendaya, and Jon Bernthal are all currently starring in two of the biggest movies in the world at the same time, which is an incredible thing to be able to say. Holland is Telemachus in The Odyssey, Zendaya is Athena, Bernthal is Menelaus. Then all three of them turn around and anchor the biggest domestic opening weekend ever recorded.

Doomsday is next, and I’m more excited for it than I’ve been for a Marvel movie in a long time.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is in theaters now. See it in Dolby, see it in ScreenX, see it in IMAX. Just go see it with a crowd.

I’ll be there again.

Seth Rogen… RIP 😔 (kind of)

So yeah… Seth Rogen “died” in The Boys Season 5, Episode 5. Naturally, I thought it’d be hilarious to make a dramatic “in memoriam” post about it. Turns out… not everyone got the joke.

Jokes aside, this episode was actually one of the strongest of the season so far. Instead of sticking to the usual structure, it leans into a chaotic, almost anthology-style format, jumping between different characters across one day.

And somehow… it works.

Why the anthology format worked

It’s wild, it’s messy, and it moves fast, but in a good way.

Up until now, the season felt like it was building slowly. This episode changes that. You can feel everything starting to come together heading into the final stretch.

We even get a perspective from Terror, which honestly felt like a deep cut for longtime fans. It’s these kinds of details that make the show stand out even five seasons in.

Is now the time to binge?

If you haven’t started The Boys yet, now’s actually a great time. You’ve got five seasons to binge, plus Gen V, with more spin-offs on the way.

New episodes drop Tuesday night at midnight Pacific Time (technically early Wednesday) on Amazon Prime Video.

If you’re watching this season, I’m curious: what did you think of Episode 5? And if you’re not watching yet… what’s stopping you?

bodyHtml:
To give context, I hated the first Mortal Kombat. So going into this, I had pretty low expectations.

I saw Mortal Kombat 2 early at the premiere, and hype factor aside, I ended up having a really good time with it. This was the first time in a while that I caught myself leaning forward in my seat, cheering, and honestly being a little embarrassed at how into it I was.

The movie starts off in a very similar way to the first one, with something big and exciting that immediately gets the audience hyped. And because of that, I got nervous. The first movie did the exact same thing. It hooked everyone with a great opening, even released that extended intro online, and then completely fell apart.

So once that opening sequence passed, I genuinely thought, “Here we go again.”

But this time, it doesn’t fall off. It keeps the momentum going. It ramps up and just keeps moving.

What stood out to me the most is that it doesn’t waste time and doesn’t rely on heavy exposition. It introduces Johnny Cage and the rest of the characters quickly, gives you just enough to understand them, and then gets straight into the action.

And that’s where the movie really works. It actually feels like a fighting game.

The structure is simple in the best way. Fights start, they play out, and then we move on. It almost feels like there’s an in-game system pushing things forward. Characters show up, handle what they need to handle, and the movie keeps moving without overcomplicating anything.

At times, it honestly felt like I was watching high-level matches play out in real time, which made the whole experience even more fun.

Another thing I appreciated is that nobody feels safe. There are real stakes, with characters on both sides getting taken out, and it keeps you guessing the entire time. That unpredictability adds a lot to the experience.

It also makes me more interested in where this goes next. If they do a Mortal Kombat 3, there’s a lot of potential to keep building on this.

As for the characters, Cole is definitely improved. He’s handled much better here than he was in the first movie, and he gets exactly what the character needed.

Karl Urban as Johnny Cage is perfect. He fully commits to the role, and it works. I genuinely can’t see anyone else playing this version of the character.

At the screening, I was sitting behind Jack Quaid, and I could hear him reacting during Karl Urban’s scenes. That added to the experience, because you could tell people were really enjoying what he was doing with the character.

Karl Urban just gets it. He understands exactly what Johnny Cage is supposed to be.

Scorpion also has his moment, and it’s still a great one. But unlike the first movie, where he felt like the main focus, here he’s more of a highlight rather than the centerpiece. And honestly, that works better for the overall movie.

If anything, it shows how much stronger the full package is this time around.

Overall, this honestly feels like the blueprint for how fighting game movies should be made. Keep the story simple, focus on the action, and don’t lose sight of what makes the source material fun.

I already posted a full review on YouTube if you want more detailed thoughts, but yeah, this was a fun time.

And if you’re a fan of Mortal Kombat, this is definitely worth watching.
